title: Comparative Advantage
body: In 1817 David Ricardo showed that two countries gain from trade even if one is better at producing everything. What matters is the relative cost of what each gives up; his example was wine and cloth in Portugal and England.

title: The Invisible Hand
body: Adam Smith used the image in The Wealth of Nations in 1776. The idea is that individuals pursuing their own interest in a working market can promote the common good without intending to. The phrase appears only once in the book but became a symbol of market economics.

title: Keynesian Economics
body: In his General Theory (1936), John Maynard Keynes argued that an economy can get stuck with high unemployment when total demand is too weak. His conclusion, that governments can stabilise the economy through fiscal policy, shaped post-war policy.

title: The Wall Street Crash of 1929
body: Share prices on Wall Street collapsed in October 1929. The crash opened the Great Depression, the deepest economic crisis of the industrial era, which changed views on the role of the state in the economy.

title: The Bretton Woods System
body: At a 1944 conference the Allies agreed on fixed exchange rates tied to the US dollar, which was in turn convertible into gold. The IMF and the World Bank were founded there. The system broke down in the early 1970s after the US ended the dollar's convertibility into gold.

title: Tulip Mania
body: In the Netherlands in the 1630s, prices of tulip bulbs rose steeply and then collapsed in 1637. It is often cited as one of the first speculative bubbles, although historians now think its scale has been exaggerated.

title: The Oldest Central Bank
body: Sweden's Riksbank, founded in 1668, is the world's oldest central bank still in operation. It grew out of Stockholm's Banco, which had issued some of Europe's first banknotes.

title: Supply and Demand
body: The price of a good settles where the quantity buyers want equals the quantity sellers offer. Alfred Marshall compared supply and demand to the two blades of a pair of scissors: neither alone determines the price.

title: Opportunity Cost
body: The true cost of any choice is the value of the best alternative given up. An hour spent studying costs not only the time but whatever else that hour could have produced. The concept is central to economic reasoning.

title: The Quantity Theory of Money
body: The theory links the money supply to the price level: if money grows faster than the output of goods and services, prices tend to rise. Milton Friedman built on it to argue that inflation is ultimately a monetary phenomenon.

title: Compound Interest
body: With compound interest, interest is earned on previously earned interest, so growth accelerates over time. The 'rule of 72' gives a quick estimate: divide 72 by the annual percentage rate to get the number of years it takes for money to double.

title: Das Kapital
body: Karl Marx published the first volume of Das Kapital in 1867. He argued that profit comes from surplus value, the difference between what workers produce and what they are paid, and that capitalism contains the seeds of its own crisis. His ideas shaped 20th-century politics.

title: The 2008 Financial Crisis
body: Losses on US subprime mortgages spread through a global financial system loaded with debt and complex securities. The bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers in September 2008 triggered a panic and the deepest recession since the 1930s.

title: Gross Domestic Product
body: GDP measures the market value of all final goods and services produced in a country over a period. Simon Kuznets helped develop national accounts in the 1930s, and himself warned that GDP is not a measure of welfare.

title: Moral Hazard
body: Moral hazard arises when someone protected from the consequences of risk takes more risk. Insurance is the classic example; in finance, banks considered 'too big to fail' may take more risk if they expect to be rescued.

title: The Phillips Curve
body: In 1958 the New Zealand-born economist Bill Phillips found an inverse relationship between unemployment and the rate of wage increases in Britain over almost a century. Policymakers came to treat it as a menu: a little more inflation could buy lower unemployment. Milton Friedman and Edmund Phelps argued that the trade-off would vanish once people came to expect inflation, and the stagflation of the 1970s seemed to prove them right.

title: The Silver of Potosí
body: In 1545 the Spanish found an enormous silver deposit at Cerro Rico, a mountain in what is now Bolivia. Worked largely by indigenous labourers conscripted under the mita system, often in deadly conditions, Potosí grew into one of the largest cities of the Americas. Its silver flowed to Spain and onwards to Asia, financing Spanish power and Europe's trade with China.

title: The Market for Lemons
body: In 1970 George Akerlof showed how markets can break down when sellers know more than buyers. In a used-car market where buyers cannot tell good cars from bad 'lemons', they will pay only an average price, which drives owners of good cars away until mostly lemons remain. His work founded the economics of asymmetric information, which helps explain warranties, brands and compulsory insurance.

title: The Spice Trade
body: Pepper, cloves, nutmeg and cinnamon were among the most valuable goods in world trade for centuries, and cloves and nutmeg originally grew only on a few islands of the Moluccas in present-day Indonesia. The desire to reach these sources directly drove Portuguese, Spanish, Dutch and English voyages to Asia. Control of spice production became a goal of European colonial power, sometimes pursued with extreme violence.

title: India's 1991 Liberalisation
body: In 1991 India faced a balance-of-payments crisis, with foreign reserves enough for only a few weeks of imports. The government of Prime Minister Narasimha Rao, with Manmohan Singh as finance minister, devalued the rupee, cut tariffs and dismantled much of the 'Licence Raj' of industrial permits. The reforms marked India's turn from state-led planning towards a more open market economy and were followed by faster growth.

title: The Marginal Revolution
body: In the early 1870s William Stanley Jevons in England, Carl Menger in Austria and Léon Walras in Switzerland independently argued that value depends on marginal utility, the extra satisfaction from one more unit of a good. This resolved the old paradox of why water, essential to life, is cheap while diamonds are dear. Their work moved economics away from labour theories of value and laid the foundations of modern microeconomics.

title: The Lewis Dual-Sector Model
body: In 1954 the St Lucian economist Arthur Lewis described developing economies as having a traditional agricultural sector with surplus labour and a modern capitalist sector. As the modern sector grows, it can draw workers from agriculture without raising wages much, until the surplus is used up. Lewis shared the 1979 Nobel memorial prize in economics, becoming the first Black laureate in a category other than peace.

title: Price Elasticity of Demand
body: Price elasticity of demand measures how strongly the quantity bought responds to a change in price. Demand for necessities with few substitutes, such as fuel in the short run, is inelastic, so higher prices barely reduce purchases, while demand for goods with close substitutes is elastic. The concept, formalised by Alfred Marshall, helps explain why governments tax goods such as tobacco and how firms set prices.

title: Cacao Beans as Currency
body: In Mesoamerica, cacao beans served as a form of money alongside lengths of cotton cloth. In the Aztec world they were used for small purchases in great markets such as Tlatelolco and were also paid as tribute. Spanish accounts describe counterfeit beans made by filling empty husks with earth, and cacao continued to circulate as small change in parts of colonial Mexico.

title: Gresham's Law
body: Gresham's law states that 'bad money drives out good': when two coins have the same legal value but different metal content, people spend the debased coin and hoard the better one. It is named after the 16th-century English financier Sir Thomas Gresham, although Nicole Oresme and Nicolaus Copernicus had described the effect earlier. The name was given in the 19th century by the economist Henry Dunning Macleod.

title: Prospect Theory
body: The psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky proposed prospect theory in 1979 to describe how people actually make decisions under risk. People judge outcomes as gains or losses relative to a reference point, and losses loom larger than equivalent gains. Their work helped found behavioural economics, and Kahneman received the Nobel memorial prize in economics in 2002, after Tversky's death.

title: Debasement of the Roman Coinage
body: Roman emperors repeatedly reduced the silver content of the denarius and its successor coins to stretch limited bullion and pay their armies. During the crisis of the 3rd century AD the silver coinage was debased until it was little more than bronze with a thin silver wash. Prices rose sharply and trust in the currency collapsed, a classic case of inflation caused by debasing money.

title: Diminishing Returns
body: The law of diminishing returns states that adding more of one input, such as labour, to a fixed amount of another, such as land, eventually yields smaller and smaller increases in output. Classical economists including David Ricardo and Thomas Malthus used it to explain rising rents and the limits to food production. It underlies much economic reasoning about costs and production.

title: The Islamic Gold Dinar
body: In the 690s the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik replaced Byzantine- and Persian-style coins with a new gold dinar and silver dirham bearing Arabic religious inscriptions instead of images. The standardised coinage helped unify the economy of an empire stretching from North Africa to Central Asia. The dinar became one of the leading trade currencies of the medieval Mediterranean and Middle East.

title: The Malthusian Trap
body: In 1798 Thomas Malthus argued that population tends to grow geometrically while food supply grows only arithmetically. Any rise in living standards would therefore be absorbed by population growth until famine, disease or restraint brought it back down. His model fits much of pre-industrial history, but the sustained growth of productivity since the Industrial Revolution allowed much of the world to escape the trap.

title: The China Shock
body: After China joined the World Trade Organization in 2001, its exports of manufactured goods surged. The economists David Autor, David Dorn and Gordon Hanson found that the parts of the United States most exposed to Chinese import competition suffered lasting losses of manufacturing jobs and lower wages. Their research on this 'China shock' challenged the assumption that workers displaced by trade easily find other work.

title: The Drain of Wealth Theory
body: Dadabhai Naoroji, an Indian economist and politician, argued in the late 19th century that British rule was draining India's wealth. Through payments such as pensions and salaries of British officials and interest on debt, a large share of India's revenue flowed to Britain without return. His book Poverty and Un-British Rule in India (1901) shaped Indian nationalist economic thought.

title: The 1997 Asian Financial Crisis
body: In July 1997 Thailand was forced to abandon the peg of the baht to the US dollar after speculative attacks. Panic spread to Indonesia, South Korea, Malaysia and other economies that had borrowed heavily in foreign currencies, and their currencies and stock markets collapsed. The IMF's rescue packages, with conditions of austerity and reform, were highly controversial, and Indonesia's crisis contributed to the fall of Suharto in 1998.

title: The Arthashastra
body: The Arthashastra is an ancient Indian treatise on statecraft, economic policy and military strategy, traditionally attributed to Kautilya, adviser to the emperor Chandragupta Maurya. It discusses taxation, state control of mines and trade, market regulation and the management of the treasury. Many scholars think the surviving text was compiled and revised over several centuries, so its date and authorship are debated.

title: Inflation Targeting
body: In 1990 New Zealand became the first country to give its central bank an explicit inflation target, under the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act of 1989. The bank was made independent in pursuing a low inflation range agreed with the government, and its governor was held accountable for meeting it. The approach spread to many central banks around the world, which commonly aim for inflation of about 2 per cent.

title: Indian Calicoes and the Calico Acts
body: In the 17th century, cheap and colourful cotton textiles from India, called calicoes after the port of Calicut, became highly fashionable in Europe. English wool and silk producers lobbied against them, and Parliament restricted them and then, in 1721, banned the use of most printed cotton cloth. Historians have argued that this protection, and the challenge of imitating Indian cloth, helped spur the mechanised British cotton industry.

title: The Resource Curse
body: Many studies have found that countries rich in oil or minerals often grow more slowly and are governed worse than resource-poor ones, a pattern called the resource curse. One mechanism is 'Dutch disease', named in 1977 after the Netherlands' experience following its natural gas discoveries: resource exports push up the currency and hurt other exports such as manufacturing. Volatile prices and corruption add to the problem, though countries such as Norway and Botswana show it can be avoided.

title: The Rochdale Pioneers
body: In 1844 a group of weavers and other workers in Rochdale, England, opened a cooperative shop selling flour, butter, sugar and oatmeal. Their Rochdale Principles, including open membership, one member one vote and the sharing of surplus among members according to their purchases, became the basis of the modern cooperative movement. Cooperatives built on these ideas spread worldwide in retail, farming, banking and housing.

title: Microfinance and the Grameen Bank
body: In 1976 the Bangladeshi economist Muhammad Yunus began lending small sums to poor villagers, mostly women, who had no access to banks. His Grameen Bank relied on groups of borrowers who supported one another, instead of on collateral. Yunus and the bank shared the 2006 Nobel Peace Prize, though later studies found microcredit's effect on poverty more modest than early supporters had hoped.

title: Public Goods
body: A public good is non-excludable, meaning no one can be prevented from using it, and non-rival, meaning one person's use does not reduce what is available to others. National defence, street lighting and basic research are standard examples. Because people can benefit without paying, markets tend to under-provide such goods, a free-rider problem that Paul Samuelson formalised in 1954 and that justifies much government spending.

title: The Solow Growth Model
body: In 1956 Robert Solow, and independently Trevor Swan in Australia, showed that adding capital alone cannot sustain growth, because each extra machine adds less output than the last. In their model, long-run growth in income per person comes from technological progress. Solow found that much of the growth in US output per worker could not be explained by more capital, a remainder known as the Solow residual.

title: The Discourses on Salt and Iron
body: In 81 BC the Han court of China held a debate over the state monopolies on salt and iron set up under Emperor Wu. Officials defended them as a source of revenue for defence, while Confucian scholars argued that the state should not compete with the people for profit. The record of the debate, the Discourses on Salt and Iron, is a classic early statement of the argument between state intervention and free enterprise.

title: The Gold Standard
body: Under the gold standard, a country's currency was convertible into a fixed amount of gold. Britain formalised it after the Napoleonic Wars, and in the 1870s many other major economies followed, creating fixed exchange rates that supported trade and investment. It tied governments' hands in recessions, however, and most countries abandoned it during the Great Depression of the 1930s.

title: Mercantilism
body: Mercantilism was the dominant economic outlook of European states from the 16th to the 18th centuries. It held that national wealth and power depended on accumulating gold and silver, so governments sought trade surpluses through tariffs, colonies and monopolies. Adam Smith attacked it in The Wealth of Nations, arguing that a nation's wealth lies in what it produces, not in its stock of precious metals.

title: The Waqf
body: A waqf is an endowment under Islamic law: property is dedicated in perpetuity, and its income supports a religious or charitable purpose. Waqfs funded mosques, schools, hospitals, fountains and caravanserais across the Islamic world, and at times held a large share of urban property. Some historians argue that the model influenced the development of charitable trusts in medieval Europe, though this is debated.

title: Bank Runs and Deposit Insurance
body: A bank run happens when depositors fear a bank will fail and rush to withdraw their money, which can bring down even a sound bank, since most deposits have been lent out. Waves of runs closed thousands of US banks in the early 1930s. In 1933 the United States created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation to guarantee deposits, and runs on insured banks became rare.

title: Cowrie Shell Money
body: Cowrie shells, above all from the Maldives, served as money across large parts of Asia and Africa for centuries. Durable, hard to counterfeit and easy to count, they circulated as small change in Bengal and in West Africa, where they arrived through trans-Saharan and later European trade. Huge imports by European traders in the 18th and 19th centuries, including cheaper East African cowries from the 1840s, caused cowrie inflation, and colonial authorities eventually replaced them with coins.

title: The Physiocrats
body: The Physiocrats, a group of 18th-century French thinkers led by François Quesnay, are often regarded as the first school of economists. They held that only agriculture produced a net surplus, and Quesnay's Tableau économique (1758) traced how this surplus circulated between social classes. Their call for free trade in grain and a single tax on land influenced Adam Smith.

title: The Washington Consensus
body: The economist John Williamson coined the term in 1989 for ten policy reforms that Washington-based institutions such as the IMF, the World Bank and the US Treasury were urging on Latin American countries. They included fiscal discipline, trade liberalisation, privatisation and deregulation. The term came to stand for market-oriented reform in general, and critics blamed it for imposing austerity on developing countries as a condition of loans.

title: Diocletian's Edict on Maximum Prices
body: In 301 AD the Roman emperor Diocletian issued an edict fixing maximum prices for hundreds of goods and services, from grain to wages, on pain of death. It was meant to curb the inflation that had followed the debasement of the coinage. According to the Christian writer Lactantius, goods vanished from the markets, and the edict was soon ignored, making it a classic early example of the failure of price controls.

title: Bitcoin
body: In 2008 a person or group using the name Satoshi Nakamoto published a design for Bitcoin, a digital currency that works without a central bank or other trusted intermediary. Transactions are recorded on a public ledger, the blockchain, maintained by a decentralised network of computers. Bitcoin launched in 2009 and inspired thousands of other cryptocurrencies, though economists debate whether such volatile assets can serve well as money.

title: Limited Liability
body: Under limited liability, shareholders can lose only what they invested in a company, not their personal assets. Britain made it widely available to ordinary companies through laws passed in 1855 and 1856, and other industrial countries adopted similar rules. By making it safer for many small investors to buy shares, it allowed the large-scale raising of capital that built railways and industrial corporations.

title: Economies of Scale
body: Economies of scale arise when the average cost of each unit falls as output grows, for example because fixed costs are spread over more units or larger plants allow more specialisation. They help explain why industries such as car manufacturing and power generation tend to be dominated by large firms. Where they are very strong, a single firm can supply a market most cheaply, creating a 'natural monopoly' that governments often regulate.

title: Sen on Famines
body: In Poverty and Famines (1981), the Indian economist Amartya Sen argued that famines are often caused not by a lack of food but by the collapse of people's ability to obtain it. In his analysis of the Bengal famine of 1943, food supply was not unusually low, but rising prices and lost earnings left millions unable to buy enough. Sen also argued that famines do not occur in functioning democracies with a free press, and he received the 1998 Nobel memorial prize in economics.

title: The Bank of England
body: The Bank of England was founded in 1694 as a private company to lend money to the government of William III for its war with France. It gradually took on the roles of a central bank: managing the national debt, issuing banknotes and acting as banker to other banks. Its creation, alongside a reliable system of public borrowing, helped Britain finance its wars more cheaply than its rivals.

title: Nash Equilibrium
body: A Nash equilibrium is a situation in a game where no player can do better by changing strategy alone, given the strategies of the others. The American mathematician John Nash proved in 1950 that such an equilibrium exists in a wide class of games. The concept became central to game theory, which economists use to analyse competition, bargaining, auctions and arms races.

title: The Euro
body: The euro was launched as an electronic currency in 1999 and as notes and coins in 2002, replacing national currencies such as the Deutschmark, the French franc and the Italian lira. Monetary policy for the member states passed to the European Central Bank in Frankfurt. Countries joining were meant to meet convergence criteria on inflation, deficits and debt laid down in the Maastricht Treaty of 1992.

title: The Harvester Judgment
body: In 1907 Justice Henry Bournes Higgins of Australia's Commonwealth Court of Conciliation and Arbitration ruled on whether the Sunshine Harvester works paid 'fair and reasonable' wages. He defined such a wage as one enough for an unskilled labourer to support a wife and three children in frugal comfort. The judgment established the principle of a basic wage based on need, which shaped Australian wage-setting for decades.

title: The Ever-Normal Granary
body: Chinese states kept public granaries that bought grain when harvests were good and prices low, and sold it when harvests failed and prices rose. The 'ever-normal granary' was established under the Han dynasty and revived by many later dynasties. The idea of using buffer stocks to stabilise prices influenced US farm policy in the 1930s.

title: Dead Capital
body: In The Mystery of Capital (2000), the Peruvian economist Hernando de Soto argued that the poor in developing countries hold large assets, such as houses and land, that they cannot use as collateral because they lack formal legal title. He called these assets 'dead capital'. His work inspired land-titling programmes in many countries, though later research found that formal titles alone often did less than expected to unlock credit.

title: Conspicuous Consumption
body: In The Theory of the Leisure Class (1899), the American economist Thorstein Veblen argued that the wealthy buy expensive goods largely to display their status. For such goods a higher price can make them more desirable, not less. The phrase 'conspicuous consumption' and the idea of 'Veblen goods' entered both economics and everyday language.

title: The Indian Ocean Trade
body: Long before European ships arrived, the Indian Ocean hosted one of the world's great maritime trading systems. Using the seasonal reversal of the monsoon winds, Arab, Persian, Indian, Malay, Chinese and Swahili merchants exchanged textiles, spices, gold, ivory, porcelain and horses between East Africa, Arabia, India and China. Ports such as Calicut, Malacca, Kilwa and Aden thrived on this largely decentralised commerce.

title: Purchasing Power Parity
body: Purchasing power parity holds that, over the long run, exchange rates should adjust so that the same basket of goods costs the same in different countries. The Swedish economist Gustav Cassel developed the modern version around the time of the First World War. Economists use PPP exchange rates to compare living standards across countries, since market exchange rates tend to understate incomes in poorer countries.

title: The Price Revolution
body: Between the late 15th and the early 17th centuries, prices in Western Europe rose several-fold after a long period of relative stability. Contemporaries such as Jean Bodin blamed the influx of American silver and gold; later historians have added population growth and coin debasement as causes. The episode is a key test case for the quantity theory of money.

title: The CFA Franc
body: The CFA franc was created in 1945 for France's colonies in Africa. After independence most former French colonies in West and Central Africa kept it, in two regional versions pegged first to the French franc and then to the euro, with convertibility guaranteed by the French Treasury. Supporters credited it with low inflation, while critics saw it as a lasting form of French control over African monetary policy.

title: Quantitative Easing
body: Quantitative easing is a policy in which a central bank creates money to buy large quantities of financial assets, usually government bonds, to lower long-term interest rates when short-term rates are already near zero. The Bank of Japan pioneered it in 2001. After the 2008 crisis it was adopted on a large scale by the US Federal Reserve, the Bank of England and later the European Central Bank.

title: Oikonomia and Chrematistics
body: The word 'economics' comes from the Greek oikonomia, the management of a household. Aristotle distinguished this natural art of providing for needs from chrematistics, the pursuit of money-making for its own sake, which he regarded as limitless and suspect. He also condemned lending at interest as making money breed money, an argument that shaped medieval Christian thinking on usury.

title: The Maghribi Traders
body: The Maghribi traders were Jewish merchants based in North Africa, notably in Tunisia and Fustat (Old Cairo), who traded across the Mediterranean in the 11th century. Their letters and accounts survive in the Cairo Geniza, a synagogue storeroom where documents were kept rather than destroyed. The economist Avner Greif argued that they kept overseas agents honest through a coalition in which cheats were collectively shunned, a classic study of how trade can work without courts, though other historians have challenged his interpretation.

title: Externalities
body: An externality is a cost or benefit that falls on people outside a transaction, such as pollution from a factory or the wider protection given by vaccination. Because buyers and sellers do not take it into account, markets produce too much of goods with harmful externalities and too little of those with beneficial ones. The British economist Arthur Pigou proposed in 1920 taxing harmful activities to correct this, the idea behind modern carbon taxes.

title: Creative Destruction
body: The Austrian-born economist Joseph Schumpeter popularised the term creative destruction in Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy (1942). He argued that capitalism advances through waves of innovation by entrepreneurs, in which new products, technologies and firms destroy old ones. For Schumpeter this process, rather than price competition, was the essential fact about capitalism.

title: The Dojima Rice Exchange
body: In Osaka, merchants traded rice and rice receipts at the Dojima exchange, which the Tokugawa shogunate officially recognised in 1730. Traders there dealt in standardised contracts for future delivery, settled in cash, so Dojima is often described as the first organised futures market. Rice was central to Japan's economy, since samurai stipends and land taxes were measured in it.

title: Say's Law
body: Say's law, associated with the French economist Jean-Baptiste Say, is often summarised as 'supply creates its own demand'. The idea is that producing goods generates the income to buy other goods, so a general glut of everything is impossible. Keynes rejected it in the 1930s, arguing that savings can go unspent and leave an economy stuck with too little demand.

title: Import Substitution Industrialisation
body: After the Second World War many Latin American countries, influenced by the Argentine economist Raúl Prebisch and the UN Economic Commission for Latin America, tried to industrialise by replacing imports with domestic production behind high tariffs. Prebisch argued that countries exporting raw materials faced worsening terms of trade against manufactured goods. The strategy built industries but often left them inefficient, and it was largely abandoned in the 1980s.

title: Rent-Seeking
body: Rent-seeking is the pursuit of wealth by capturing a share of existing income, for example by lobbying for subsidies, tariffs or exclusive licences, rather than by creating new value. Gordon Tullock analysed it in 1967 and Anne Krueger gave it its name in 1974. Because the resources spent on rent-seeking produce nothing, economists see it as a hidden cost of monopoly and of some government intervention.

title: Hayek and the Knowledge Problem
body: In his 1945 essay 'The Use of Knowledge in Society', Friedrich Hayek argued that the knowledge needed to run an economy is dispersed among millions of people and cannot be gathered by any central planner. Prices act as signals that coordinate their actions without anyone needing to see the whole picture. The argument became central to the case against central planning.

title: Paper Money in Song China
body: Merchants in Sichuan began issuing paper notes called jiaozi as receipts for heavy iron coins, and in the early 1020s the Song government took over their issue. These were the first government-issued paper money in the world. Later governments, especially under the Yuan and early Ming, printed notes to excess, and the resulting inflation discredited paper currency in China for centuries.

title: The Coase Theorem
body: Ronald Coase argued in 1960 that if property rights are clearly defined and bargaining is costless, the parties will negotiate an efficient outcome whoever holds the rights. Since bargaining is rarely costless, his deeper point was that transaction costs and legal rules matter. In 1937 Coase had also explained why firms exist: organising some activities inside a firm is cheaper than using the market for everything.

title: The Division of Labour
body: Adam Smith opened The Wealth of Nations (1776) with a pin factory, where splitting the work into about eighteen operations let ten workers make tens of thousands of pins a day. Specialisation raises productivity through greater skill, time saved and the invention of machinery. Smith added that the division of labour is limited by the extent of the market, linking growth to trade.

title: From GATT to the WTO
body: The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, signed in 1947, set rules for trade and organised successive rounds of negotiations that sharply reduced tariffs on manufactured goods. Its Uruguay Round created the World Trade Organization in 1995, with a stronger system for settling disputes between countries. The core principle is non-discrimination: a tariff cut granted to one member should apply to all.

title: The Corn Laws
body: Britain's Corn Laws, tightened in 1815, imposed tariffs on imported grain to protect landowners' incomes. Manufacturers and the Anti-Corn Law League, led by Richard Cobden and John Bright, argued that they raised the price of bread. Their repeal in 1846 under Robert Peel split the Conservative Party and marked Britain's turn to free trade.

title: The Single Whip Tax Reform
body: In the late 16th century the Ming government of China, under the grand secretary Zhang Juzheng, extended the 'single whip' reform, which consolidated many land taxes and labour obligations into a single payment in silver. The reform simplified taxation and accelerated the use of money throughout the Chinese economy. China's resulting demand for silver drew in vast quantities of the metal from Japan and the Americas.

title: The Stone Money of Yap
body: On the Pacific island of Yap, in Micronesia, large stone discs called rai, quarried on Palau and carried back by canoe, served as a store of value and a means of payment. Many were too heavy to move, so ownership passed by common agreement while the stones stayed in place. Economists including Milton Friedman have used Yap to show that money rests on shared belief rather than physical possession.

title: The Trans-Saharan Gold Trade
body: From around the 8th century, camel caravans linked North Africa with the West African kingdoms of Ghana, Mali and Songhai. Gold from West African fields went north, while salt mined in the Sahara and goods from the Mediterranean went south. The trade financed powerful states and trading cities such as Timbuktu, and West African gold was a major source of metal for medieval Islamic and, later, Italian gold coins.

title: China's Reform and Opening
body: From 1978, under Deng Xiaoping, China began dismantling central planning. Farmers were allowed to sell surplus output under the household responsibility system, and special economic zones such as Shenzhen were opened to foreign investment. The reforms launched decades of rapid growth that lifted hundreds of millions of people out of extreme poverty.

title: Henry George's Land Value Tax
body: In Progress and Poverty (1879), the American writer Henry George asked why poverty persisted alongside economic progress. His answer was that landowners captured the gains of growth through rising land rents, and he proposed replacing other taxes with a single tax on the value of land. Many economists regard land value taxation as efficient, because the supply of land cannot shrink in response to the tax.

title: The Eurozone Debt Crisis
body: From late 2009, revelations that Greece's deficit was far larger than reported set off a crisis of confidence in the debt of several eurozone governments. Greece, Ireland, Portugal and Cyprus received bail-outs tied to austerity, and Spain's banks also needed help. Unable to devalue or set their own interest rates, members faced painful adjustments, and the crisis eased after the ECB's president Mario Draghi pledged in 2012 to do 'whatever it takes' to preserve the euro.

title: Fiat Money
body: Fiat money has value because a government declares it legal tender and people accept it, not because it can be exchanged for gold or another commodity. Since the United States ended the convertibility of the dollar into gold in 1971, all major currencies have been fiat money. Its value depends on trust in the institutions that issue it, which is why the credibility of central banks matters so much.

title: Double-Entry Bookkeeping
body: In double-entry bookkeeping, every transaction is recorded twice, as a debit in one account and a credit in another, so the books must always balance. The method developed among Italian merchants in the late Middle Ages and was first described in print by Luca Pacioli in 1494. It made errors easier to detect and is the foundation of modern accounting.

title: Debt Cancellation in Mesopotamia
body: Rulers in ancient Mesopotamia periodically proclaimed edicts, known in Babylonia as misharum, that cancelled certain debts and freed people who had fallen into debt bondage. Such decrees were issued by Babylonian kings in the first half of the second millennium BC, continuing a tradition attested in Sumer centuries earlier. Historians often see them as attempts to stop debt from ruining the free peasants on whom armies and taxes depended.

title: Ujamaa in Tanzania
body: With the Arusha Declaration of 1967, Tanzania's president Julius Nyerere launched ujamaa, a form of African socialism named after the Swahili word for 'familyhood'. Banks and major industries were nationalised, and millions of rural people were moved, often under pressure, into collective villages. The policy brought gains in literacy and national unity, but agricultural output suffered and it was gradually abandoned in the 1980s, especially after Nyerere stepped down in 1985.

title: The South Sea Bubble
body: The South Sea Company, granted a monopoly of British trade with Spanish America, took over much of the national debt in 1720 in exchange for its own shares. Its share price soared in a speculative frenzy and collapsed later that year, ruining many investors. A parallel bubble in John Law's Mississippi Company burst in France the same year.

title: The Federal Reserve
body: The United States created the Federal Reserve in 1913, after repeated banking panics, notably that of 1907. Its structure combines a Board of Governors in Washington with twelve regional Reserve Banks. Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz later argued that its failure to prevent the collapse of the banking system in the early 1930s turned a recession into the Great Depression.

title: The Dutch East India Company
body: Founded in 1602, the Dutch East India Company (VOC) held a monopoly on Dutch trade with Asia and the power to wage war, make treaties and govern territory. Its shares were traded continuously in Amsterdam, and it is often described as the first publicly traded company, a model for later corporations. From its base at Batavia, now Jakarta, it dominated the spice trade for much of the 17th century.

title: Hyperinflation
body: Hyperinflation is extremely rapid inflation, often defined as prices rising by more than 50 per cent a month. Famous cases include Germany in 1923, Hungary after the Second World War and Zimbabwe in the late 2000s. It usually arises when governments finance large deficits by printing money, and it wipes out savings and can destroy trust in a currency within months.

title: The Medici Bank
body: Founded in Florence in 1397 by Giovanni di Bicci de' Medici, the Medici Bank became one of the most powerful financial houses of 15th-century Europe. It had branches in cities such as Rome, Venice, Geneva, Bruges and London, managed papal finances, and used bills of exchange to move money across borders. Its wealth underpinned the family's political power and their patronage of Renaissance art.

title: The Latin American Debt Crisis
body: In the 1970s Latin American governments borrowed heavily from Western banks flush with oil exporters' deposits. When US interest rates soared and commodity prices fell, Mexico announced in August 1982 that it could not service its debt, and the crisis spread across the region. The 1980s became known in Latin America as the 'lost decade' of falling incomes, ending with debt write-downs under the Brady Plan.

title: Barter and the Double Coincidence of Wants
body: Barter requires a 'double coincidence of wants': each party must want exactly what the other offers. Economists since Adam Smith have explained the invention of money as a way around this problem. Anthropologists, however, have found few if any societies that relied mainly on barter; many early economies ran instead on credit, gifts and obligations.

title: OPEC and the 1973 Oil Shock
body: The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries was founded in Baghdad in 1960 by Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela to coordinate oil policy. In 1973, during the Arab–Israeli war, Arab oil producers imposed an embargo on countries supporting Israel, and oil prices roughly quadrupled within months. The shock ended the post-war boom in the West and revealed the economic power of oil exporters.

title: Fractional-Reserve Banking
body: In fractional-reserve banking, banks keep only a fraction of their deposits as reserves and lend out the rest. When the borrowed money is spent and deposited again, it can be lent again, so the banking system as a whole creates money. The practice is often traced to goldsmiths in 17th-century London, who found they could lend out part of the gold left with them for safekeeping.

title: The Four Asian Tigers
body: Hong Kong, Singapore, South Korea and Taiwan industrialised at exceptional speed from the 1960s to the 1990s, moving from poverty to high incomes within about a generation. They combined high saving and investment, education and export-oriented growth, though South Korea and Taiwan also relied heavily on state guidance of industry. Economists still debate how much of their success came from markets and how much from government policy.

title: The Sherman Antitrust Act
body: Passed by the US Congress in 1890, the Sherman Act outlawed contracts and conspiracies in restraint of trade and attempts to monopolise a market. It was a response to the power of trusts such as Standard Oil, which was broken up under the act in 1911. It became the foundation of American competition law, which inspired similar laws elsewhere.

title: The Manila Galleons
body: From 1565 to 1815 Spanish galleons sailed across the Pacific between Acapulco in Mexico and Manila in the Philippines. They carried American silver westwards and returned with Chinese silks, porcelain and other Asian goods bought from merchants in Manila. The route linked the Americas and Asia directly for the first time and is often seen as the start of a truly global trade network.

title: Hawala
body: Hawala is a system for transferring money through a network of trusted brokers without physically moving cash. A customer pays a broker in one city, a partner broker elsewhere pays the recipient, and the brokers settle between themselves later. Rooted in medieval trade across the Islamic world and South Asia, it has long been used for remittances, though regulators have worried about its use to evade controls.

title: The Tragedy of the Commons
body: When a resource such as a pasture or fishery is open to all, each user gains from using more while the cost of depletion is shared, so the resource tends to be overused. The ecologist Garrett Hardin popularised the idea as 'the tragedy of the commons' in 1968. Elinor Ostrom later showed that many communities manage shared resources successfully through their own rules, work that made her in 2009 the first woman to win the Nobel memorial prize in economics.

title: The Invention of Coinage
body: The first coins were struck in Lydia, in western Anatolia, around the 7th century BC, from electrum, a natural alloy of gold and silver. A stamped coin of guaranteed weight spared traders from weighing metal at every exchange. The idea spread quickly through the Greek world, and coinage also arose independently in China and India.

title: Soviet Five-Year Plans
body: From 1928 the Soviet Union under Stalin replaced markets with central planning, setting production targets in successive Five-Year Plans. Heavy industry grew rapidly, but at enormous human cost, including the forced collectivisation of agriculture and famine. The model of a state-planned economy was later adopted by many communist countries, where it struggled with shortages, poor quality and weak incentives.

title: M-Pesa and Mobile Money
body: M-Pesa, launched in Kenya in 2007 by the mobile operator Safaricom, lets people store and transfer money using simple mobile phones, with cash handled by a network of local agents. It spread rapidly among people without bank accounts and transformed how Kenyans pay bills and send money to relatives. It became a model for mobile money services across Africa and other developing regions.

title: The Sogdian Merchants
body: The Sogdians, an Iranian people centred on Samarkand and Bukhara, dominated long-distance trade across Central Asia from roughly the 4th to the 8th century. Their merchant communities stretched from Persia to northern China, and their language served as a lingua franca of the overland routes. Letters left by Sogdian traders reveal networks of credit, partnership and agency spanning thousands of kilometres.

title: The Lender of Last Resort
body: In Lombard Street (1873), the journalist Walter Bagehot argued that in a financial panic the central bank should lend freely to solvent banks, against good collateral, at a high rate of interest. This would stop panics without rewarding imprudence. 'Bagehot's rule' became a guiding principle for central banks in crises, including in 2008.

title: The Infant Industry Argument
body: The infant industry argument holds that new industries may need temporary protection from foreign competition until they become efficient enough to compete. Alexander Hamilton made the case in his Report on Manufactures to the US Congress in 1791, and the German economist Friedrich List developed it in the 19th century. It remains one of the most debated exceptions to the case for free trade.
